gaps.sentence: ___ of what he says is nonsense.
gaps.explanation: 'Most of what he says' is the pattern 'most of + noun clause'; 'the most of' is wrong.

gaps.sentence: I haven't got ___ cash on me — I'll pay by card.
gaps.explanation: 'Any' is the normal quantifier in negative sentences; 'haven't got no cash' would be a double negative.

gaps.sentence: Only ___ people attended the talk, which was disappointing.
gaps.hint: countable plural; 'only a few' is the natural pattern
gaps.explanation: 'Only a few people' is the standard way to say a small number; 'only few' is not used.

gaps.sentence: Hardly ___ came to the afternoon lecture.
gaps.explanation: 'Hardly anyone' is already negative — do not add 'no one'.

gaps.sentence: The lecture was ___ attended than the organisers had hoped.
gaps.explanation: 'Well attended' compares with the adverb: less well attended.

gaps.sentence: The hall was so crowded that ___ found a seat.
gaps.hint: a crowded hall means no one succeeded
gaps.explanation: 'So crowded that nobody found a seat' matches the logic of the sentence; 'anybody' cannot be the subject of an affirmative clause.

gaps.sentence: She has two children. One lives in Leeds, and ___ lives in York.
gaps.hint: one of a pair of two
gaps.explanation: 'One ... the other ...' is the pattern for exactly two; 'another' would imply more than two.

gaps.sentence: This year the festival attracted ___ visitors than in 2024.
gaps.explanation: 'Fewer' is the comparative for countable plurals like visitors; 'less' is for uncountables.
